title: Survey Reveals Working Parents' Constant Struggle: 'No Way to Be Two Things at Once'
summary: Amber Petersen knows the feeling all too well. One moment she's scheduling meetings at the small law firm where she works as a legal assistant in Mason City, Iowa. The next, a school nurse calls—her child is sick, and she has to drop everything. 'I feel like that tug of war is constantly on my mind of where I need to be—if I am missing out as a mom, or if I am disappointing somebody at work,' she told NPR. 'There's just no way to be two things at once and give 100% at both.' A new survey from the Pew Research Center confirms that Petersen's struggle is widespread. The survey of 2,242 working parents—primarily those in families where both parents work full-time—found that two-thirds of working mothers report they can't give 100% at home, and just over half say they can't give their all at work. Fathers are feeling the strain too: half say they can't give 100% at home, and about a third say the same about work. 'We see that parents are facing lots of demands from both work and family, and that the boundary between those is often blurry,' said Pew senior researcher Rachel Minkin. The findings come as the share of families with both parents working full-time has surged from 31% in 1975 to 52% today, according to Pew's analysis of census data. For Petersen, staying home isn't an option. Even with two incomes, her family is just getting by. She's grateful her employer is understanding when family issues arise—she can leave on a dime. But she pays a price: she only gets paid for the hours she works, with no paid sick leave. Her husband, who paints industrial trucks in a factory, would be penalized for leaving work unexpectedly. The survey found that more than half of lower-income parents, and single mothers especially, are highly worried about losing pay if they have to leave work for family reasons. Black and Hispanic parents worry more about this than white and Asian parents. Petersen says paid sick leave would help enormously, as would more affordable childcare. A couple of years ago, she had to let her two daughters, then 11 and 12, stay home alone because a summer program cost a couple thousand dollars—more than the family could afford. Nearly half of working parents in the survey reported difficulty finding summer care for school-aged kids. It's a relentless juggling act, and parents across the country are hoping for structural changes that ease the burden.
why_it_matters: This story goes beyond one family; it exposes systemic cracks in the American economy. When parents cannot afford to be present for a sick child or to pay for summer care, it raises big questions about what kind of support systems society owes its workers — questions that will still be debated when you enter the workforce.

background_read: The United States is one of the only wealthy countries without a federal law that guarantees paid sick leave for workers. This leaves millions of people like Amber Petersen in a precarious position when a child falls ill.
Since the 1970s, the number of two‑parent families where both adults work full‑time has nearly doubled, from 31% to 52%. Economic pressure and changing gender roles are major drivers of this shift.
The Pew Research Center is a nonpartisan (non‑political) American think tank that has conducted rigorous surveys on family and work life for decades.
The U.S. Census Bureau’s decennial count and annual surveys provide the data that researchers use to track trends in family structure and employment.
Childcare costs in the U.S. have risen dramatically; a summer program can easily cost a couple thousand dollars per child, creating impossible choices for lower‑income families like Petersen's.

perspectives.description: Some employers, researchers, and policymakers see the growing attention on work‑family conflict as a push toward better policies like paid leave and flexible hours. They argue that supporting parents leads to healthier, more loyal employees and benefits businesses and families alike.

Working parents, especially single mothers and low‑income households, bear an unsustainable burden. The lack of paid sick leave and affordable childcare forces impossible trade‑offs — leaving a child home alone, losing pay, or even risking a job — and deepens inequality along race and class lines.

Sociologists see the blurring of work and family boundaries not as a personal failing but as a result of broad economic shifts, including the end of single‑income stability, the rise of the 24/7 work culture, and policy gaps in care infrastructure. It is a structural tension that individual effort alone cannot solve.

Survey data like this can fuel legislative pushes for federal paid sick leave and subsidized childcare, but deep political divisions mean change is uncertain. The next generation — today’s teenagers — may inherit a workplace that looks very different if they demand reforms. In the meantime, more states and companies are experimenting with local solutions as a testing ground.
